summary: The paper studies Bayesian coresets through general asymptotic bounds on posterior approximation quality measured by forward/reverse KL divergence. Its main contribution is a broad theoretical framework that goes beyond prior analyses limited to exponential families or strongly log-concave smooth models. The paper derives: (i) general lower bounds (Theorems 3.3 and 3.5) under mild local regularity and posterior concentration assumptions, showing that coreset quality is fundamentally controlled by mismatch in local gradient behavior and curvature; and (ii) a general upper bound (Theorem 5.3) based on a generalized subexponentiality condition on centered log-likelihoods. These results are then specialized to obtain several notable consequences: importance-weighted coresets require size M proportional to N to keep KL bounded (Corollaries 4.1 and 4.2), any coreset method needs at least d support points in a locally d-dimensional identifiable neighborhood (Corollary 4.3), and subsample-optimize methods can achieve bounded KL with polylogarithmic coreset size under suitable alignment and subexponentiality assumptions (Corollary 6.1). The theory is supported by experiments on two deliberately challenging synthetic models—a multimodal/unidentifiable Cauchy location model and a heavy-tailed unidentifiable logistic regression model—where empirical KL trends match the predicted asymptotics.
strengths_text: Addresses an important and under-theorized problem: general guarantees for Bayesian coreset quality beyond restrictive model classes.; Provides both lower and upper bounds, which is significantly stronger than papers offering only one-sided analysis; the lower bounds are especially valuable because they reveal fundamental limitations of coreset constructions.; The lower-bound machinery is technically elegant: Lemma 3.1 reduces KL analysis to localized overlap quantities, and Theorems 3.3/3.5 connect posterior error to weighted gradient mismatch in a way that is interpretable and broadly applicable.; The results yield concrete and impactful algorithmic insights, especially the negative result for importance-weighted coresets and the positive result for subsample-optimize methods.; Assumptions are substantially weaker than much prior work: the paper explicitly accommodates multimodality, unidentifiability, and heavy tails, which materially broadens relevance.; Theoretical claims are carefully stated, with full proofs in the appendix and clear separation between general results and application corollaries.; Empirical validation is well chosen: the two synthetic examples are not trivial sanity checks but stress-test settings that violate common assumptions in earlier analyses.; Figures 2 and 3 provide convincing qualitative agreement between theory and observed KL scaling.; The paper is well written and logically organized; the progression from generic lemmas to asymptotic theorems to algorithm-specific corollaries is easy to follow.; Corollary 4.3 is conceptually strong because it gives a dimension-dependent impossibility result for any coreset construction, not just a specific algorithm.
weaknesses_text: The main results are asymptotic and do not provide explicit finite-sample constants or practically computable error estimates, which may limit immediate operational use.; The upper-bound framework relies on subexponentiality and, for the subsample-optimize guarantee, an alignment condition in Eq. (6); these assumptions are plausible but may be difficult to verify in new models without case-by-case work.; Empirical evaluation is limited to two synthetic models, so the paper does not demonstrate behavior on larger real-world Bayesian inference tasks.; Algorithm 3 is analyzed abstractly via an optimization oracle over KL-constrained weights on a sampled support; the practical approximation used in experiments (NNLS on discretized log-likelihoods) is not itself theoretically analyzed in this paper.; Some assumptions, especially posterior concentration condition (A5) and the moment/alignment conditions in later corollaries, are technically involved and may be hard for non-specialists to map onto concrete models.
methodological_flaws_text: I did not identify a clear fatal flaw in the scientific logic. The main theorem statements are internally consistent with the proof strategy, and the paper is careful to distinguish assumptions needed for lower versus upper bounds.; A notable limitation is that the empirical validation is only qualitative with respect to asymptotic rates; it does not directly test the sharpness of constants or the necessity of each assumption. This is not a correctness issue, but it weakens empirical substantiation of practical tightness.; Theorem 5.3 and Proposition 5.4 establish existence-style upper bounds via subexponentiality, but the practical usefulness depends on constants (e.g., beta) that are not generally characterized. Thus the upper-bound side is more existential than constructive.; Corollary 6.1 depends on the alignment probability condition in Eq. (6), which is assumed rather than derived generically. This means the positive guarantee for subsample-optimize methods is somewhat conditional compared with the stronger impossibility-style lower bounds.; The experiments use synthetic settings and approximate optimization procedures rather than exact KL minimization, so they validate trends rather than the full formal setup of the theory.
